title: EDUCATION | 5.25.26 Too Many A's, Too Few A-'s
author: Underwood, Terry
source: Learning to Read, Reading to Learn (Substack)
summary: Harvard's faculty voted 458-201 to cap A grades at 20% of enrollment per class beginning fall 2027, responding to data showing over half of all undergraduate grades were A's and nearly 85% fell in the A range. The article analyzes this decision through information theory: a letter grade is a maximally lossy compression operator that projects a semester of heterogeneous performance onto a five-point ordinal scale, discarding all qualitative texture by design. When 85% of grades occupy the A range, the symbol has lost its only function—distinguishing position in a distribution—because there is no longer a meaningful not-A to contrast against. The companion measure replacing GPA with average percentile rank for internal honors is, the author argues, an explicit admission that the letter grade was never adequate for comparative ranking work. The cap treats the compressed output as the problem while leaving the upstream cause—changes in instructor judgment over twenty years—completely unaddressed. The author concludes the decision is a public confession that the grading system is, and will remain, theater.
points: * A letter grade is a maximally lossy compression operator—projecting rich performance data onto a five-point ordinal scale, discarding all qualitative information by design. * When 85% of Harvard grades fall in the A range, the letter A has lost its only function: ordinal distinction through contrast with a meaningful not-A. * The companion measure switching internal honors to percentile rank is an implicit admission that the letter grade was always inadequate for comparative ranking. * The cap treats the compressed output signal as the problem while leaving the upstream cause—changes in instructor judgment over decades—completely unaddressed. * The decision amounts to a public confession that the external-facing grading system is, and will remain, theater while a real ranking system operates underneath.
quotes: A letter grade is, by design, a maximally lossy compression operator. It takes some underlying field of student performance — a semester's worth of papers, exams, participation, problem sets, each themselves already compressions of something else — and projects it onto an ordinal scale with five points (or eleven, counting pluses and minuses).

An A means something to the extent that not-A is a live possibility for the student receiving it. When 85 percent of grades are A-range, the letter A has lost its ordinal information because there's no longer a meaningful 'not-A' to contrast against.

If you take the phrase at face value and ask what qualitative content a letter grade actually carries, the honest answer is: none. What a letter grade carries is a position in a distribution — and the entire signaling value of that position depends on the distribution having dispersion.

Percentile rank reintroduces the dispersion that the letter compression destroyed. Which means the committee's actual diagnosis, stripped of the courage-and-rigor diction, is something like: the letter grade is a bad instrument for the comparative-ranking purpose we've been pretending it serves.
This decision is a confession that the public-facing grading system is, and will remain, theater.

The cap operates at the level of the compressed signal without information beyond its ritual significance. So if there's a qualitative failure anywhere, it is upstream of the grade, in whatever has happened to the relationship between instructor reading and instructor judgment over the last twenty years, and the cap addresses that not at all.
